# PicoCalc Shapes

*README.MD file mostly generated by Anthropic's Claude AI because Thomas Dzubin hates documenting code.  LOL*

A small shape-drawing demo for the ClockworkPi PicoCalc, built on the
Raspberry Pi Pico SDK. Author: Thomas Dzubin.

Six filled shapes sit on the 320x320 LCD in two rows of three: a thin
rectangle, a square and a triangle across the top, then a pentagon, a
five-pointed star and a circle across the bottom. Each shape can be grown,
shrunk, rotated and coloured on its own, and remembers its own size, angle
and colour while you move on to another one.

The display driver only offers a solid rectangle, so everything else is
rasterised by the program: the circle as a stack of one-pixel rows, and the
other shapes through a scanline polygon fill that also copes with the
concave star. All the maths is integer only (fixed-point sine and cosine
from a table), so it needs no `math.h` and no floating point, which suits the
RP2040.

## Controls

| Key           | Action                                                          |
|---------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------|
| LEFT / RIGHT  | select the previous / next shape (a white box marks the selection); in colour mode, step the selected shape's colour around the rainbow |
| + / -         | grow / shrink the selected shape (stops at 1x1 pixel)           |
| UP / DOWN     | move through the shapes and pickers: from a top-row shape DOWN goes to the shape below, then to the hue strips, the saturation bar and the value bar; UP goes back |
| F1            | step through shape-select, colour-select (plain rainbow), colour-select (improved rainbow), then back to shape-select |
| F2            | toggle saturation mode: LEFT / RIGHT change the selected shape's saturation, 0 to 100 percent in steps of 2 |
| F3            | toggle value (brightness) mode: LEFT / RIGHT change the selected shape's value, 0 to 100 percent in steps of 2 |
| ?             | show the help screen, which also appears when the program starts; any key continues |
| F4 / F5       | rotate the selected shape 5 degrees counter-clockwise / clockwise |
| ESC or Q      | leave for the PicoCalc UF2 Loader menu                          |
| ~ (SHIFT + `) | reboot into BOOTSEL (USB drive) mode                            |

There are two rainbow strips, stacked above the status line. The top one is
the plain hue wheel. The lower one is an improved wheel: each colour channel's
linear ramp is passed through sqrt(v * (510 - v)), so the colours between the
primaries (yellow, cyan, magenta and the blends around them) are not dimmer
than the primaries. Both strips use the same hue for the same column. In the
first colour mode a small arrow above the top strip points at the exact stripe
the selected shape is drawn in; in the second colour mode an arrow below the
lower strip does the same. A shape keeps the wheel it was last coloured from. The status line under the strip shows
the selected shape's name, size and rotation.
The pickers are stacked: the two hue strips on top, then the saturation bar,
then the value bar, with the colour line under them. The saturation bar runs
from white (no saturation) at the left end to the full colour at the selected
shape's hue at the right end; press F2 to select it. The value (brightness)
bar runs from black at the left end to the full colour at the right end; press
F3 to select it. Arrows mark the selected shape's hue, saturation and value at
all times, and the picker being edited is outlined in white, as the selected
shape is. Each shape keeps its own saturation and value, and each bar shows
the colours the shape can have with the other setting held. The colour line
shows the selected shape's colour as its RGB565 fields in hex: R and B from 00
to 1F, G from 00 to 3F.

Leaving asks the loader for its menu through the watchdog scratch registers
(constants in `loader_const.h`); if the program was flashed straight to the
chip with no loader installed it simply restarts, and on a PC it closes.

## Files

- `picocalc-shapes.c` - the whole program. The header comment block at the top
  is the design reference (drawing primitives, rotation, selection and colour
  modes, screen layout).
- `shapes_const.h` - every constant and data table (colours, sizes, screen layout, keys, sine table, shape names).
- `loader_const.h` - the values used to hand control back to the UF2 Loader.
- `CMakeLists.txt`, `pico_sdk_import.cmake` - firmware build config.
- `desktop/` - Desktop (SDL2) build for Windows and Linux: its own
  `CMakeLists.txt` plus a small shim of the driver API, so the same
  `picocalc-shapes.c` runs on a PC.
- `picocalc-text-starter-main/` - vendored copy of `picocalc-text-starter` (see
  Third-party below).
- `CHANGELOG.md` - notable changes, by version.

## Building

VS Code Pico extension (Compile / Run), or from a terminal with
`PICO_SDK_PATH` set:

    cmake -B build -G Ninja
    ninja -C build

Output: `build/shapes-<chip>.uf2` (`<chip>` is `RP2350` or `RP2040`, matching
the board). Flash by copying to the `RPI-RP2` drive; hold BOOTSEL on power-up,
or press `~` (SHIFT + backtick) in the app. The build also copies the `.uf2` to
the top-level folder as `shapes-RP2350.uf2` / `shapes-RP2040.uf2` (by board),
so both chips' builds sit side by side.

### Windows

From an MSYS2 UCRT64 shell with SDL2 installed:

    cmake -S desktop -B build-windows -G Ninja
    ninja -C build-windows

Output: `shapes-Windows.exe` in the top-level folder. SDL2 is linked
statically, so it is a single file with no `SDL2.dll`. `~` simply closes the
program.

### Linux

The same source builds on Linux with the SDL2 development package installed
(for example `sudo apt install libsdl2-dev`). Unlike the Windows build, SDL2 is
**not** linked in statically: the program links `libSDL2` dynamically, and the
build copies that library next to the executable as `libSDL2-2.0.so.0`, where
the executable finds it through an `$ORIGIN` run-path. Keep the two files
together.

    cmake -S desktop -B build-linux
    cmake --build build-linux

Output: `shapes-Linux` and `libSDL2-2.0.so.0` in the top-level folder.

## Third-party

[`picocalc-text-starter`](https://github.com/BlairLeduc/picocalc-text-starter)
by **Blair Leduc** (LCD, audio and south-bridge keyboard drivers) is vendored
in `picocalc-text-starter-main/` and used under its own license (see the
`LICENSE` file in that folder).

The vendored copy is Blair Leduc's `picocalc-text-starter` as it was on 2026-10-18
(commit `85a002e`, "Upgrade to SDK 2.3.1"), with **four small local fixes** that
are not in his repository yet:

1. In `picocalc-text-starter-main/drivers/fat32.c`, `fat32_write()` no longer walks
   the cluster chain, allocating a cluster at a cluster-aligned end of file, before
   it allocates the clusters the write needs. That walk could leave a cluster
   unreachable (a leak). A write of zero bytes returns at once.
2. In the same file, `fat32_dir_read()` copies the last part of a long file name of
   248 to 255 characters as far as it fits; upstream drops that part.
3. In `picocalc-text-starter-main/drivers/sdcard.c`, a command is not sent to a card
   that is still busy after the 0.5 s wait.
4. In `picocalc-text-starter-main/drivers/lcd.c`, `lcd_putstr()` cuts a string off at
   the right edge of the display, because the line buffer holds exactly one row of
   text.

Earlier versions of this copy carried other local changes, and those are now in
the upstream code: the search-hint fix in `get_next_free_cluster()`
([#30](https://github.com/BlairLeduc/picocalc-text-starter/pull/30)), the
deleted-entry fixes in `fat32_dir_read()` and `link_entry()`
([#32](https://github.com/BlairLeduc/picocalc-text-starter/pull/32)), the timed
busy-card wait in `sdcard.c`
([#33](https://github.com/BlairLeduc/picocalc-text-starter/pull/33)) and
`lcd_unblit()` ([#31](https://github.com/BlairLeduc/picocalc-text-starter/pull/31)).
`audio.pio` is exactly as downloaded: it now accepts 20 to 20000 Hz
([#29](https://github.com/BlairLeduc/picocalc-text-starter/pull/29)), where it used
to accept only 100 to 2000 Hz. Everything else is exactly as downloaded.
